name: REMA (Remington Evaluations)
toolCategory: Traditional mystery shopping provider, multifamily specialist

verdict.line: A multifamily-native shop shop with published per-shop pricing and every shop type we run — compete on scoring consistency, benchmarking and the coaching-to-training handoff, not on whether they can shop an apartment.

pricing.value: Public FAQ states shops run "$55 to $170 per shop" depending on level of detail and report length; rush service available for an additional charge.

positioning.value: Multifamily-focused evaluation firm offering phone, onsite and email leasing consultant evaluations plus competitor, fair housing, customer service, potential-employee and video shops, with trending, graphing and benchmarking reports.

strengths.text: Full shop-type coverage in one vendor: "phone and onsite leasing consultant evaluations as well as email shops," plus competitor, fair housing, potential-employee, customer service and video shops.
Publishes a per-shop price range on the public site, which makes them easy for a buyer to budget against.
Offers trending, graphing and benchmarking reports alongside individual shop reports.
Multifamily is the core vertical; the same firm also serves mini storage, moving, retail, real estate and automotive.

gaps.text: Published standard turnaround is slow: "Normally a report will take about 2 to 3 weeks," and the FAQ notes delays of 30+ days are possible when shopper or target scheduling breaks down.
Public site describes shop delivery and reporting; it does not describe linking shop results to assigned training or courseware.

whyWeWin: Shop scores land in the same platform as the training assignment, so a low fair housing score becomes a course on that person's plate rather than a PDF in someone's inbox.
Benchmarking is drawn from a multifamily shop dataset built over decades, not a per-client trendline.
One vendor covers phone, email, onsite and video shops alongside surveys, training and policy in a single system of record.
askThis: When a shop comes back at 60, what happens next in your process — who gets told, and what do they do that week?
How long from shop completion to a report a regional can act on? What's your contractual turnaround?
How is a shopper's score normalized across shoppers so a 78 in Dallas means the same as a 78 in Atlanta?
What are you benchmarking against — your own portfolio last quarter, or the industry?

objections.response: Price the outcome, not the shop. Ask what the shop costs plus what it costs to turn 400 shop reports into coaching that changes a score. If shops and training live in two systems, that second cost is a person's job.
So do we. The question isn't the format, it's what the video does after it's recorded — whether it's a file a manager may watch or a scored, benchmarked event that assigns the follow-up.

doNotSay: Never say they can't do video or fair housing shops — their public FAQ lists both.
Never quote their pricing as a current number in a competitive deal; the published range is a website figure, not a quote.

ms-video.note: Video shops listed among shop types.

name: MarkerHeads (Journey Reports)
toolCategory: Multifamily end-to-end prospect journey evaluation, sold as an annual audit rather than a recurring shop program

verdict.line: A once-a-year multifamily journey audit from a small branding agency — it competes for the shop budget as a one-time diagnostic, so compete on continuous measurement and the coaching loop, not on report design.

pricing.value: Not published. Site states the report is bought "Just once a year. At a familiar price" and directs buyers to contact for portfolio and property pricing.

positioning.value: "THE INDUSTRY'S ONLY END-TO-END JOURNEY EVALUATION" — an unbiased view of the prospect experience from reach through sales conversion, scored across email, text, phone, chatbot and tour, presented in a visual journey map with emotional signals at each stage.

strengths.text: Scores performance across the full channel set — email, text, phone, chatbot and tours — rather than a single shop event.
Claims 1,500 property evaluations completed for large investment groups across market rate, senior, student, active adult and new development assets.
Uses "market data and technology to model the behavior of location-specific, real in-market prospects" rather than a generic shopper script.
Output is a visual journey map with emotional signals at each stage — designed to be read by executives, not just operations.
Comes from a multifamily branding and placemaking agency, so the report lands with marketing budget holders as easily as operations.

gaps.text: Sold as an annual evaluation — the site's own framing is "Just once a year" — rather than a continuous shop program with retests.
The shop methodology is not disclosed; the site describes modeled in-market prospect behavior and characterizes the product as "like a shop on steroids" without specifying human shopper mechanics.
1–10 employee firm founded in 2023, per its vendor directory listing — a small operation relative to enterprise portfolio shop volume.
No public description of coaching linked to training assignment or of an industry benchmark dataset.

whyWeWin: An annual snapshot tells you where you stood in March; a continuous program tells you whether the coaching worked in April.
Scores feed training assignment automatically, so the diagnostic becomes an intervention.
Shop volume and delivery capacity for national portfolios, with published shop types and a consistent rubric across every property.
askThis: If the report is annual, how do you know whether the fixes you made actually moved the number?
How many shops per property per year are you doing today, and what is the retest cadence?
Who does the follow-up coaching after the journey report lands — and what do they assign?

objections.objection: The Journey Report is the only end-to-end evaluation in the industry.
objections.response: It is a strong diagnostic and the visual is genuinely good. Ask what happens between annual reports. A diagnostic once a year plus nothing in between is a photograph; you're trying to run a film.

objections.objection: It's cheaper than a full shop program.
objections.response: It should be — it's a different product. One audit versus a measured, retested coaching cycle across every community. Compare on outcome per property per year, not per report.

doNotSay: Never characterize the report as low quality or as 'not a real shop' — the methodology simply isn't disclosed publicly.
Never quote a price.

verdict.line: Flair reads every leasing call instead of sampling a few shops — it is a different product bought with the same budget, so it is a substitution risk, not a feature gap.
verdict.doInstead: Do not run this as a battlecard fight and do not try to win it by arguing shop quality — you will lose on volume math. Qualify what the buyer is actually trying to fix: if they want coverage of their own call volume, that is a product and strategy conversation, so log the deal and route it to product and strategy. Where the buyer also needs an unsolicited, unaffiliated prospect experience across onsite, video and email — which conversation intelligence of your own agents does not produce — position the two as complementary, not competing.

pricing.value: Not published; vendor directory requires a verified buyer account to view pricing. Public site offers free introductory secret shops.

positioning.value: "Flair is the conversation intelligence layer of the leasing tech stack. It reads every leasing and resident conversation...and turns them into signals teams can act on now." Site framing: "Your systems report activity, not behavior. They don't show what prospects actually experience. Flair does."

strengths.text: "Call Intelligence: Reads every call, scores agents (human and AI), and surfaces the demand underneath" — coverage of the full call population rather than a sample.
Scores AI leasing assistants as well as human agents, answering a question operators are actively asking: "Is your AI better than your team?"
"Email Shops: Synthetic leads test your follow-up and catch the breaks no one else sees" — an outbound test channel on top of passive call analysis.
"Custom Scorecards: Grade every call & email shop against your criteria, not a generic rubric."
Free introductory secret shops lower the barrier to a first engagement and get them inside accounts without a procurement cycle.
Serves BTR, multifamily, self storage, senior living and student housing; publishes named property management references including CRES and Trion Properties.
Also monitors fair housing compliance and answer rates by property and agent.

gaps.text: Coverage is calls, email, text and interaction tracking; the public product description does not include onsite or video shops of a physical leasing office.
Call intelligence reads conversations the team already handled — by construction it cannot score a prospect inquiry that was never answered, since there is no conversation to read.
The email test channel uses synthetic leads rather than a human shopper's account of the experience.
Public materials describe scoring and signals; they do not describe coaching linked to assigned training courses.

askThis: Are you trying to measure your team's own call handling, or test what an unsolicited prospect actually experiences? Those are two different jobs.

Once you know an agent is weak on objection handling, what assigns and tracks the training?

objections.objection: Flair reads every call. Why would we pay for a handful of shops?
objections.response: That's a fair question and it's not one I'm going to argue you out of. Reading every call and testing the unsolicited prospect experience are different jobs — call intelligence can only read conversations your team already had. If both matter to you, let me bring in our product team rather than trying to talk you out of the one that fits.

doNotSay: Never claim our shop quality makes conversation intelligence unnecessary — it is a different measurement, and the volume argument is not winnable.
Never assert Flair cannot do onsite or video shops as a capability claim; say their published product description covers calls, email, text and interactions.
Never quote or estimate Flair's pricing.

name: Grotto AI
toolCategory: AI conversation intelligence and real-time coaching for multifamily leasing agents

verdict.line: Purpose-built for multifamily, funded by ICONIQ, and coaching agents live on every call and tour — it displaces the reason people buy shops rather than competing with the shops themselves.
verdict.doInstead: This is not a battlecard fight. Do not try to win it by arguing shop quality or shopper training — the buyer is comparing continuous coverage against a sample and you will lose that comparison on its own terms. Qualify what they want to change, then route the deal to product and strategy with the account and the use case. Where the buyer needs an unaffiliated test of the prospect experience — including communities that never answer the phone, email follow-up and onsite behavior — say so plainly and keep the two products in separate lanes.

ownership.value: Private, venture-backed; founders Nick Deveau (CEO) and Ben Epstein (CTO), previously of EvolutionIQ

funding.value: $10M seed announced 19 February 2026, led by ICONIQ, with Asymmetric Capital Partners, Avi Dorfman (Compass co-founder) and Caren Maio (Funnel Leasing co-founder)

pricing.value: No pricing published on the public site.

positioning.value: "AI-powered sales coaching and guidance for multifamily leasing teams" — "Close more leases with Grotto's real-time, AI sales coaching, purpose-built for multifamily," covering the entire prospect lifecycle across calls, tours and written communication.

strengths.text: Purpose-built for multifamily rather than a horizontal sales tool with a multifamily page.
"Call Guidance" delivers "real-time guidance for agents on every call — helping them ask the right questions, handle objections, and book tours" — coaching during the conversation, not after it.
$10M seed led by ICONIQ (February 2026) with multifamily-native angels including Compass and Funnel Leasing co-founders.
Named enterprise customer: Weidner Apartment Homes, which manages over 70,000 units.

Publishes behavioral findings from its own conversation data — agents who laughed with a prospect were "48% more likely to convert a lead to a signed lease," and genuine curiosity correlated with "a 35% increase in conversion." These are Grotto's published claims, not independently verified.
Frames the buy in NOI terms — "recover 8 to 9 figures in NOI and asset value" — which reaches an executive budget that a shop program usually does not.

gaps.text: The product analyzes the operator's own leasing interactions and coaches its own agents; public materials do not describe an independent, unaffiliated third-party shop of the prospect experience.
Because guidance operates during calls and tours the team is already having, there is no described mechanism for evaluating an inquiry that received no response.
Public materials do not describe a human shopper network, video shops, or an industry benchmark dataset.
Traction is described publicly only as "Early customer data points to meaningful improvements in both engagement and conversion" — no published customer count or independently verified results.

askThis: Do you want to coach the conversations you're already having, or find out what happens when a prospect reaches out and nobody responds?
How does Grotto tell you about the community where the phone went unanswered all Saturday?

objections.objection: Grotto coaches our agents on every single call. Shops only sample.
objections.response: That's true, and I'm not going to argue the math. They're solving a different problem than an unaffiliated test of the prospect experience. Let me bring in our product team so we're comparing the right things rather than me making a case I can't support.

objections.objection: ICONIQ backed them — they'll win this category.
objections.response: Funding is a signal about the category, not about your portfolio. The useful question is what you're trying to change this year, and whether coverage of your own calls or an outside test of the prospect experience gets you there. Often it's both.

doNotSay: Never argue that human shops make real-time call coaching unnecessary.
Never repeat Grotto's conversion statistics as independently verified fact — they are the vendor's own published claims.
Never state that Grotto has no shopping capability as an absolute; say their public materials describe coaching of the operator's own agents.

name: Status quo — internal spot-checks and DIY comp shops
toolCategory: No vendor — regional managers doing their own spot-checks and comp shops phoned in and compiled in a spreadsheet

verdict.line: The most common competitor in the pipeline is a regional manager with a spreadsheet — respect that it works and costs nothing on paper, then compete on independence, consistency and whether anyone can prove the coaching changed the score.

pricing.value: No line-item cost. The spend is regional manager and marketing coordinator time, which sits inside payroll rather than a vendor budget.

positioning.value: "We already do this ourselves." A regional walks the property, calls a few communities as a prospect, phones competitors for rents and specials, and puts the results in a shared spreadsheet reviewed at the monthly ops meeting.

strengths.text: It is genuinely free at the point of use — no procurement, no contract, no vendor onboarding, no budget line to defend.
The person doing the evaluation already knows the property, the team, the submarket and the history, so context that a third-party shopper misses is built in.
Feedback is immediate and personal. A regional who hears a bad call can coach that afternoon rather than waiting for a report.
Comp shops phoned in by the team produce current rent and concession intelligence that also feeds pricing decisions — one activity, two uses.
Nothing is hidden behind a vendor's methodology. The operator controls exactly what gets asked and can change it the same day.
For a small portfolio with a hands-on regional, this is often sufficient — and telling that buyer otherwise is how you lose credibility.

whyWeWin: A shopper the team does not recognize gets the experience a real prospect gets; a regional the team recognizes gets the experience the team performs.
One rubric applied across every community means a 78 in one region is comparable to a 78 in another, which a spreadsheet of different people's impressions cannot deliver.
The evaluation is documented and time-stamped by a third party, which matters when a fair housing question arrives.
The score assigns the training and the retest proves it moved — the loop closes without anyone remembering to close it.
Regional manager hours spent shopping are hours not spent on occupancy, and that cost is real even though it never appears on an invoice.
askThis: How many of your communities got shopped last quarter — not planned, actually shopped?
Does the team know when a regional is shopping them? What happens to the result when they do?
If two regionals score the same call, do you get the same number?
When a shop surfaces a fair housing risk, what's the documented record six months later if someone asks?
What does a regional's day cost you, and how many of those days go into shopping and comp calls each month?
Show me the last time a low score turned into training that someone completed — where would I see that?

objections.objection: We already do this ourselves and it works fine.
objections.response: For a lot of operators it does, and I'm not going to tell you it doesn't. The two things it can't give you are independence — your team knows the regional's voice — and consistency, so scores compare across regions and over time. If neither of those is a problem for you today, keep doing what you're doing.

It's off-budget, which isn't the same thing. Count the regional hours and the comp-call hours per month. Then ask what those hours would have earned somewhere else. The question isn't whether to spend, it's what you're already spending and what you get back for it.

objections.objection: Our regionals know the properties better than any outside shopper would.
objections.response: True, and that's an advantage for coaching. It's a disadvantage for measurement — the team performs differently for someone they recognize. Use both: their judgment for coaching, an outside read for the baseline.

doNotSay: Never tell a buyer their internal process is amateur or unserious — it is usually run by the most committed operator in the building.
Never quote a savings or ROI figure for replacing internal shops; we have no sourced number for their internal cost.
Never imply their team is dishonest. The issue is that people behave differently for someone they recognize, not that anyone is cheating.

ms-human-shoppers.note: Internal staff act as shoppers; they are not an independent, unaffiliated network.

ms-phone.note: Comp calls and spot-check calls are typically the most-used method.

ms-onsite.note: Regional property walks are common, but the team knows who is visiting.

ms-video.note: Not part of a typical internal spot-check process.

ms-rubric.note: Some operators use a standard form; many rely on individual judgment. Ask.

ms-coaching.note: Coaching is immediate and personal, but linkage to assigned, tracked training is rare.

ms-full-call-analysis.note: A handful of spot-checks per period is a small sample by definition.

ms-benchmarking.note: Comparison is against the operator's own portfolio and comp set, not an industry dataset.
